title: US steelmaker shifts $500m federal hydrogen funds to upgrade coal blast furnace
description:
US steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs will use $500m in federal funds originally intended to transition its Ohio ironworks to “hydrogen-ready” operations to instead upgrade its coal-fired blast furnace.
It said the funds would now go toward a $1bn project to make upgrades to its blast furnace, install advanced material handling infrastructure, and AI-enabled process control technologies.
The firm will also look to construct a cogeneration facility to capture and use blast furnace gas to generate electricity and steam for on-site consumption.
It expects the blast furnace to be rebuilt in the first quarter of 2030.
The Inflation Reduction Act funds were awarded to Cleveland-Cliffs in 2024 to convert its Middletown blast furnace to hydrogen direct reduced iron operations.
text:
US steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs will use $500m in federal funds originally intended to transition its Ohio ironworks to “hydrogen-ready” operations to instead upgrade its coal-fired blast furnace.

Coming 14 months after the company officially abandoned its hydrogen-based steel project in Middletown, it has now established a framework to negotiate and implement a rescoping of the $500m awarded by the Biden administration.

It said the funds would now go toward a $1bn project to make upgrades to its blast furnace, install advanced material handling infrastructure, and AI-enabled process control technologies.

The firm will also look to construct a cogeneration facility to capture and use blast furnace gas to generate electricity and steam for on-site consumption.

It expects the blast furnace to be rebuilt in the first quarter of 2030.

The Inflation Reduction Act funds were awarded to Cleveland-Cliffs in 2024 to convert its Middletown blast furnace to hydrogen direct reduced iron operations.

By June last year, the project was dropped, with CEO Lourenco Goncalves citing a lack of support from the Trump administration and an additional $1.1bn required to replace its coal-fired operations.

In a statement on the new funding use, Goncalves said, “The [Department of Energy’s] support for this project is a testament to the importance of preserving the blast furnace route to produce automotive-exposed grade steels in the US, while advancing American energy dominance.”

Speaking at the Middletown Works, Vice-President JD Vance said the new programme would “protect and create tonnes of new jobs.”

The rescoping comes amid a wider retreat from Biden-era clean energy funding under the Trump administration, which has sought to redirect federal energy policy toward fossil fuels, nuclear power, and projects it considers supportive of US energy security.

In 2025, the DOE terminated hundreds of awards worth more than $11bn across two major rounds of cuts, affecting industrial decarbonisation, carbon capture, grid, and hydrogen projects. Among the casualties were the California and Pacific Northwest regional clean hydrogen hubs, which were awarded a combined $2.2bn.

The cuts have added uncertainty around the US clean hydrogen sector when developers are already contending with high costs, limited offtake, and policy uncertainty.

name: Clean Energy
title: Green‑on‑green conflicts between ecological and energy engineering along China's coast - Nature
description:
Spatially overlapping with national large-scale invasive Spartina alterniflora remediation projects, energy development inevitably triggers interactive tensions between clean energy construction and wetland ecological restoration5,6.
This Perspective synthesizes the development status of China’s tidal-flat photovoltaic industry and the latest progress in S. alterniflora ecological control.
Where conditions allow, tidal-flat photovoltaic facilities can be integrated with aquaculture-pond photovoltaics and saltpan-based photovoltaic installations13,14.
The total area of tidal-flat photovoltaic projects in the Chinese intertidal will increase rapidly in the coming decades.
As it increases, we recommend four actions to minimize this green-on-green conflict, minimize financial waste, and maximize the success of both green energy and ecological restoration.
text:
Driven by global low-carbon transformation and China’s dual-carbon strategy, tidal-flat photovoltaics have emerged as an effective offshore renewable energy approach, enabling low-carbon energy expansion1,2. Nevertheless, large-scale photovoltaic engineering significantly alters intertidal hydrological conditions, sediment dynamics and wetland ecosystem structures3,4. Spatially overlapping with national large-scale invasive Spartina alterniflora remediation projects, energy development inevitably triggers interactive tensions between clean energy construction and wetland ecological restoration5,6. Traditional research has largely discussed clean energy development benefits or wetland restoration effects independently, while ignoring the potential conflicting interactions between the two eco-friendly human activities, termed “green-on-green conflicts“7. This research gap restricts the formulation of targeted coordinated governance systems for sustainable coastal development.

This Perspective synthesizes the development status of China’s tidal-flat photovoltaic industry and the latest progress in S. alterniflora ecological control. It systematically clarifies the bidirectional conflicts between photovoltaic operation and invasive species management and identifies the physical and institutional drivers of green-on-green conflicts, as well as the practical barriers that restrict coordinated governance. We propose a multi-dimensional optimization framework covering engineering design improvement, cost accounting, institutional coordination, and cross-disciplinary collaborative planning. This study provides theoretical support and practical strategies for mitigating conflicts in coastal eco-engineering, balancing the low-carbon energy transition and wetland biodiversity conservation, and realizing the synergistic benefits of the energy transition for coastal ecological security.

Pursuant to China’s national goals of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality (the “dual‑carbon” targets), clean and low‑carbon energy engineering is expanding rapidly in the country1,8,9. Wind power, photovoltaic power generation, hydropower, nuclear power, and the relatively low‑carbon fuel, natural gas, form the core of the clean‑energy mix, with installed capacity and electricity generation continuing to increase10 (Fig. 1a). Among these sources, tidal‑flat photovoltaic facilities, a subset of offshore photovoltaics, are emerging as an important type of clean electricity generation2, with their actual constructed area reaching nearly 37,180 hectares by 2025 (Fig. 1b). The term “tidal-flat photovoltaic facilities” refers to photovoltaic power stations installed in coastal tidal flats and adjacent areas that are connected to the grid via underground cables3,11. The main advantages of tidal-flat photovoltaic stations are proximity to coastal load centers and existing grid infrastructure, which can reduce transmission distances and facilitate interconnection, and reduced competition for terrestrial land11,12. Where conditions allow, tidal-flat photovoltaic facilities can be integrated with aquaculture-pond photovoltaics and saltpan-based photovoltaic installations13,14.

In recent years, tidal‑flat photovoltaic projects have advanced rapidly in China, especially in Shandong, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, and Guangdong provinces, adopting area‑based, clustered layouts15 (Fig. 1b). These projects have created jobs in equipment manufacturing, construction, and operations and maintenance services, substantially increasing local tax revenues16. Demonstration projects are now progressing toward large‑scale deployment. This wave of tidal‑flat photovoltaic facilities is unfolding along a pathway of pilot projects, demonstration projects, large‑scale expansion, and cluster development, gradually establishing a large‑scale clean‑energy presence along China’s eastern coast17.

Human activities on the planet degrade wild landscapes into semi-wild or anthropogenic biomes18. Restoration of degraded lands aims to reverse this process. Within the intertidal zone of China, another massive ecological project, the control of the non-native grass Spartina alterniflora, is also being vigorously advanced19. Introduced in 1979 as an “engineering species” to promote siltation and shoreline stabilization, S. alterniflora expanded rapidly, significantly suppressing native salt‑marsh plants such as Scirpus mariqueter, Suaeda salsa, and Phragmites australis, reducing the availability of bird foraging and roosting sites, weakening key habitat functions for some fish and benthic invertebrate groups, promoting habitat homogenization, and substantially altering the landscape and community structure of coastal mudflats20,21.

From 2022 to 2025, five national ministries of China implemented a comprehensive control and restoration campaign, setting S. alterniflora removal targets of 90–95% in priority wetlands and estuaries, and conducting annual assessments to prevent resurgence5. Currently, most localities employ combined, integrated engineering interventions for invasive-plant control, including mechanical excavation, deep plowing with plastic‑film mulching, and enclosures or interception barriers as the primary measures, supplemented by low‑dose, targeted chemical control, and coordinated with geomorphological restoration19,22 (Fig. 1c). Monitoring has shifted from annual patrols to an integrated evaluation framework that combines satellite imagery, unmanned aerial vehicle surveys, and field transects23. In several demonstration areas, notable results have been observed: invasive cover has declined significantly, spread has been curtailed, and native community cover and ecological functions have partially recovered8,24.

Inevitably, there are places where energy projects and restoration intersect. This can at times be beneficial. Restoration sometimes improves economic activity. For example, restoring natural prairie strips improves biocontrol of pests in farmlands25. And economic activity sometimes improves restoration. For example, grazing by livestock can remove invasive species26,27. Mutually beneficial outcomes, however, are not guaranteed. Tidal-flat photovoltaic projects are likely to degrade newly restored tidal flats by limiting growth of benthic algae, altering invertebrate communities, and limiting access by waterfowl3,28. Most insidiously, tidal-flat photovoltaic projects are likely to hinder control of S. alterniflora. Many tidal‑flat photovoltaic projects are located on parts of the intertidal that substantially overlap with the potential distribution of S. alterniflora and can create eco‑engineering feedback15.

Photovoltaic arrays interfere with S. alterniflora control in three ways: (1) monitoring is hindered, because panel reflectance and shadow banding, together with mismatches in tidal timing, reduce detection and recall rates in remote‑sensing and unmanned aerial vehicle surveys, leading to omissions and delayed identification of regrowth; (2) treatment is constrained, because low under‑panel clearance, dense arrays of pilings and cables, and electrical safety restrictions preclude use of large mechanical equipment, forcing reliance on manual or small equipment spot removal within limited tidal windows, substantially increasing the cost of control per hectare; (3) pollution and re‑dispersal occur, because piles and walkways trap floating marine debris and plant litter, which can entangle with S. alterniflora residues to form floating rafts that both worsen pollution and carry propagules beyond arrays, facilitating new invasion hotspots. Thus, the persistence of S. alterniflora populations intermingled with photovoltaic structures will provide an ongoing source of propagules that will seed new invasions of S. alterniflora along the coast, making full control of S. alterniflora less likely4,29 (Fig. 1d).

At the same time, S. alterniflora regrowth may degrade the operation of photovoltaic stations. The high aboveground biomass and dense rhizome–root system of S. alterniflora trap sediment and elevate tidal‑flat microtopography, thereby reducing the effective ground clearance of photovoltaic modules30,31. In areas with abundant sediment supply, vertical accretion rates can exceed ~9.6 cm per year32,33. As vegetation and the mud surface approach or exceed the lower edge of photovoltaic modules, the risks of shading and corrosion of electrical components increase, and, under storm‑surge conditions, the likelihood of structural instability and safety hazards also increases34,35.

The parallel advance of tidal‑flat photovoltaic development and S. alterniflora control constitutes a typical ecology–energy dilemma6. In this case, the potential pitfalls to co-locating economic activity and restoration described above could be minimized by thoughtful planning. Tidal-flat photovoltaic systems represent the practical needs of the clean‑energy transition, requiring large investment and delivering significant socioeconomic benefits; S. alterniflora control is central to maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services on the coast. When the two projects intersect at the same time and in the same place, a “green‑on‑green conflict” arises as one virtuous project interferes with and undoes the activities of another7. As described above, this conflict stems from both physical processes and institutional constraints. Physically, photovoltaic shading and piles alter intertidal hydrodynamics and light and thermal regimes, creating sheltered spaces for invasive plants, thereby complicating monitoring and removal efforts. Institutionally, evaluation of energy projects prioritizes generation efficiency and returns on investment, while ecological externalities and long‑term management costs are not fully internalized, leading to an imbalance between short‑term benefits and long‑term risks. Although S. alterniflora control has achieved removal rates exceeding 90% in some areas, the absence of long‑term monitoring and spatially coordinated planning means that new rounds of photovoltaic construction can undermine S. alterniflora control efforts.

The total area of tidal-flat photovoltaic projects in the Chinese intertidal will increase rapidly in the coming decades. As it increases, we recommend four actions to minimize this green-on-green conflict, minimize financial waste, and maximize the success of both green energy and ecological restoration. (1) Engineering design optimization: optimize pile height and under-panel clearance, row spacing, and array layout to maintain access for monitoring and invasive-plant removal, and to minimize propagule and stem trapping by posts, cables, and walkways (based on a three-dimensional management and control system integrating manual patrol and real-time monitoring). Where appropriate in already invaded areas, shading-intensive layouts could be evaluated as a complementary suppression option, but should be weighed against restoration goals and access needs. (2) Improve cost accounting: include invasive‑species control and ecological compensation into life‑cycle assessments and internalize ecological management costs (the relevant costs would rise by ~30% beyond original estimates) into the cost of electricity. (3) Strengthen institutional and regional coordination: establish joint review and information‑sharing mechanisms among energy, ecological, and local authorities to clarify spatial boundaries between control and construction areas. (4) Implement cross-disciplinary project-level co-design: convene managers, engineers, ecologists, and economists to translate ecological constraints into design standards and mitigation plans and to evaluate trade-offs between power generation, restoration goals, and long-term management. Within such a framework of sound planning and broad collaboration, the conflict between green energy and ecological restoration can be more effectively managed, enabling the energy transition and ecological protection to coexist and yield joint benefits on the same intertidal flats.

These proposals for optimizing engineering and institutional measures face obvious practical constraints in actual implementation. First, institutional fragmentation restricts governance efficiency. Coastal management in China involves overlapping jurisdictions of energy, marine, natural resource, and ecological departments. Divergent administrative objectives and insufficient cross-departmental coordination often lead to policy disconnection and inconsistent implementation. Second, conflicting policy priorities create structural dilemmas. Local governments generally prioritize short-term renewable energy expansion and economic growth as core performance indicators, while wetland restoration and biodiversity conservation are long-term public goods. This imbalance frequently makes ecological goals subordinate to energy construction needs. Third, heterogeneous stakeholder interests result in inevitable conflicts. PV enterprises pursue maximum economic benefits and large-scale land exploitation, whereas ecological authorities focus on wetland protection and invasive species control. Local governments prioritize industrial development, while coastal residents are more concerned about long-term livelihoods and ecological services. Such multi-agent interest divergence produces persistent governance trade-offs. Fourth, economic constraints limit practical implementation. A more extensive zoning process, closer supervision of individual projects, and mandatory ecological design requirements all increase short-term construction and supervision costs. The mismatch between rising upfront economic inputs and lagged ecological benefits reduces the willingness of local authorities and enterprises to fully implement optimized governance strategies. Being aware of these constraints and taking steps to address them will make attempts to mitigate green-on-green conflicts more successful.

(NASDAQ: EOSE) (Eos), America's leading innovator in designing, manufacturing, and providing zinc-based long-duration energy storage (LDES) systems sourced and manufactured in the United States, today announced a non-exclusive strategic software and hardware collaboration agreement that combines WATTMORE's patented Intellect Operate EMS/PPC/SCADA platform with Eos' Z3 long-duration energy storage systems.

As part of this agreement, Eos has committed to deploy WATTMORE's Intellect Operate Energy Management System (EMS) and Power Plant Controller (PPC) for select customer projects and support integration of WATTMORE's EMS platform with Eos' DawnOS™ and Z3 technology. Designed, engineered, and operated by WATTMORE's Denver-based team, the platform combines FEOC- and BABA-compliant hardware with Intellect Operate software to provide a pre-integrated controls option for Eos customers. The collaboration expands the controls ecosystem around Eos' Z3 systems, helping streamline deployment while supporting Eos' strategy of delivering more complete energy storage solutions around its technology.

"Energy storage systems depend on battery technology, controls, and software working together as a single operating environment," said Jonathan W. Postal (JW), WATTMORE's Founder and CEO. "Our collaboration with Eos brings together complementary capabilities across those layers, creating a stronger foundation for customers."

Eos and WATTMORE will integrate Intellect Operate with Eos' DawnOS and Z3 systems. DawnOS provides battery-level monitoring, control, and optimization for Z3 systems, while WATTMORE's software manages system dispatch, energy optimization, and grid interaction. Completing integration upfront creates a repeatable model and simplified path from project design to deployment.

"Customers are looking for integrated solutions that reduce complexity and simplify deployment," said Nathan Kroeker, Chief Commercial Officer of Eos. WATTMORE and Eos have previously partnered on large-scale projects, including most recently a 3 MW/12 MWh energy storage project for the Nebraska utility Lincoln Electric System. NEW YORK, NY, UNITED STATES, August 24, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Today Crux, the capital platform for the clean economy, announced the close of a $215 million tax equity investment to support the Pleasant Prairie Solar Energy Center, a 240-megawatt utility-scale solar project in Franklin County, Ohio, developed and owned by Invenergy, North America’s largest privately held independent power producer and energy infrastructure innovator.

Currently under construction, the Pleasant Prairie Solar Energy Center will support approximately 300 construction jobs, generate reliable electricity that will be delivered to the local grid, and drive more than $230 million in local economic investment over the life of the project. A third-party offtaker will receive the clean energy credits associated with the new generation capacity of the facility, which is expected to begin commercial operations in 2027.

The investment was underwritten and structured by Crux Capital Securities, Crux's registered broker-dealer. The hybrid tax equity investment was made through a Crux-managed vehicle and is designed to efficiently monetize the project's federal investment tax credits while supporting the deployment of new utility-scale solar generation.

As demand for reliable, affordable electricity continues to boom across the United States, tax equity remains a foundational financing tool for large-scale clean energy infrastructure. Increasingly, developers are seeking integrated capital solutions that combine tax equity with transferable tax credits, debt capital, and other financing products to optimize project economics and accelerate the buildout of new power.

text:
BlocPower is shutting down.

The energy transition darling of the Biden-era, which championed affordable building electrification and clean energy retrofits for 12 years, is liquidating its assets and returning money to investors, reported Latitude Media.

At the height of BlocPower’s success, the company had contracts for building, community and municipal retrofits in New York, Denver, San Jose, Calif., and elsewhere (see, “Inside BlocPower’s mission to upskill workers and green New York City buildings”). BlocPower raised $154 million in debt and equity in 2023.

But the Brooklyn-based company struggled to deliver at scale, and some clients complained that BlocPower’s revenue model wasn’t aligned with building owners’ and tenants’ interests. Co-founders Keith Kinch and Donnel Baird resigned from the company in 2024. Kinch declines to comment; Baird couldn’t be reached.

Investor losses

In the liquidation, BlocPower’s senior investors, including Goldman Sachs and VoLo Earth Ventures, will be repaid first; investors from BlocPower’s crowdfunding campaigns would only be repaid after senior investors are made whole.

“Management does not currently expect that any assets will remain available to distribute to unsecured creditors,” Latitude Media reported, citing a BlocPower letter to investors.

Other investors included Kapor Capital, Builders Vision, Microsoft’s Climate Innovation Fund, Andreessen Horowitz and recently retired NBA-star Russell Westbrook.

text:
Award will fund expansion of production capacity, creating more than 100 operational jobs and strengthening U.S. supply chain independence for American mobility and defense applications

SAN LEANDRO, Calif., Aug. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Coreshell Technologies announced that it has been selected by the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Manufacturing Deployment Office (MDO) for a $50 million award under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

The award will fund the expansion of Coreshell's manufacturing facilities, establishing the first U.S. gigafactory dedicated to producing lithium-ion batteries with anodes made entirely from metallurgical silicon (MGS) that supplants graphite, the most challenging Chinese critical mineral to remove from battery supply chains.

Coreshell's patented technology leverages abundant MGS to completely replace graphite, a critical mineral that is heavily concentrated in China (>93% of global supply). Coreshell pairs this innovation with dry-coating cathode technology developed with subrecipient AM Batteries. Together, the two companies will build out approximately 2 gigawatt-hours of electrode manufacturing capacity and 1.5 gigawatt-hours of cell assembly capacity.

The project is expected to create more than 100 domestic jobs across production, technical, and administrative roles, with hiring phased alongside construction and equipment ramp-up. These batteries will not only comply with the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), but they will be the first scalable cells in the US to fully eliminate supply chain vulnerabilities from China.

"This award is about more than building a factory. It's about liberating the batteries that power America from a supply chain we don't control," said Jonathan Tan, CEO and co-founder of Coreshell. "Today, the anode material in nearly every lithium-ion battery traces back to Chinese graphite processing. By proving that domestically sourced metallurgical silicon can replace that graphite at scale, we're giving the U.S. automotive and defense industries a path to energy storage that isn't hostage to a foreign supply chain. This DOE award lets us build that capability right here in the US."

Domestic mineral producers, including Coreshell's supply partner Ferroglobe, already produce more than 100,000 tons of MGS per year, giving Coreshell's approach a secure, scalable U.S. feedstock in a segment of the battery supply chain that is almost entirely foreign-controlled today. By anchoring both anode active material and cell production onshore, the project is designed to reduce U.S. reliance on foreign batteries for the electric vehicle industry while also supporting specialized applications for the U.S. military, where secure, domestically sourced battery supply chains are a growing national security priority.

AM Batteries will contribute its Powder-to-Electrode™ dry coating process for cathode manufacturing as a subrecipient, eliminating solvent-based wet coating and the associated solvent-recovery and management infrastructure. AM Batteries' dry electrode manufacturing reduces capital costs, operating costs, and safety risk while enabling higher performance cells.

"This project is about proving that a 100% domestically produced high-performance battery cell can be cost-competitive with mass-market cells from Asia." said Hieu Duong, CTO of AM Batteries. "The U.S. will not win by simply replicating existing technologies or the status quo; we must create fundamental advantages in manufacturing and materials. By combining AMB's platform with Coreshell's MGS anode technology, we can lower cost, improve performance, and help build a globally competitive battery industry in the West."

About Coreshell Technologies: Coreshell Technologies is a San Leandro, California-based technology company that develops high-performance batteries that fully replace Chinese graphite anodes with domestically sourced metallurgical silicon (MGS). Its patented technology delivers higher performance than conventional battery cells at significantly lower cost.

About AM Batteries: AM Batteries (AMB) is revolutionizing battery manufacturing with its breakthrough dry electrode technology platform. Founded in 2020 and headquartered in Massachusetts, AMB's proprietary Powder-to-Electrode™ process eliminates toxic solvents and energy-intensive drying, dramatically simplifying one of the costliest and resource-intensive steps in battery manufacturing. The process enables lower-cost, higher-performance, and more sustainable batteries. AMB provides battery manufacturers with a turnkey solution combining production equipment, process technology, and manufacturing know-how, giving partners everything needed to deploy the platform in their own production environments.

text:
By Martin McConnell

The largest battery manufacturer in North America is adding to its production capacity even further, as LG Energy Solution began production at its new facility in Lansing, Michigan Aug. 18.

Manufacturing both EV batteries and large-format systems for energy storage projects, the new facility “will play a key role in broadening Michigan’s manufacturing base,” according to representatives. The plant is aiming for more than 35 GWh of annual battery production capacity once at full-scale production.

More specifically, the plant will manufacture lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells for energy storage systems, the company says. With cells integrated by LG Energy Solution Vertech, the complete systems will go toward utility, grid-scale energy storage, as well as other commercial and industrial markets.

David Kim, CEO of LG Energy Solution, says the plant’s opening is “a defining milestone” for the firm.

“Lansing will produce advanced batteries that support not only the future of mobility, but also America’s growing energy infrastructure and digital economy,” he says. “We are strengthening America’s battery ecosystem, expanding our manufacturing footprint and reaffirming our long-term commitment to the United States.”

In addition to large-scale battery systems, the new plant will produce nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cells for Toyota. The company says the new cells will power a bevy of the auto giant’s EV models, with the process entirely manufactured on U.S. soil between LG and Toyota’s efforts.

“Domestic battery production is foundational to America’s energy future – reducing dependence on foreign adversaries, driving good-paying American jobs and advancing the American Energy Dominance Agenda,” says U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who attended the plant’s grand opening ceremony.

“Michigan is uniquely positioned to help lead this effort with its skilled workforce, manufacturing expertise and the industrial capabilities needed to strengthen America’s domestic battery supply chain.”

Committing to the Mitten

LG Energy Solution has invested more than $2 billion into the Lansing facility since 2022. Now employing 900 team members, and with plans to nearly double that number in the coming years, the company is fully committing to Michigan, company representatives say.

“The state’s skilled workforce is a great fit for our high impact industry, and we expect to continue our partnership with Michigan well into the 21st century,” says Dae-sik Choi, president of LG Energy Solution Michigan. “The jobs at this facility pay well, offer great benefits and require creativity and problem solving at all levels.

“Unlike many other high-tech industries, battery making creates jobs for everyone, from hourly workers to advanced degree holders.”

The facility’s opening also marks LG Energy Solution’s second plant in the state, according to the company. The South Korean company has invested north of $5 billion total in the Great Lakes State since 2010, and expects to be a top 50 employer across the state by the end of 2026.

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer says the state hopes to keep working with LG not only to bolster its economy, but create opportunities in the American energy sector as a whole.

“Michigan is open for business and creating good-paying jobs building the future of cars, chips, and batteries,” she says. “LG Energy Solution has called Michigan home for more than 20 years, and we’re proud to see that investment continue with the start of production at its Lansing facility. This project will create up to 1,700 good-paying jobs, helping more working families make it in Michigan. It’s part of our historic work to invest in clean energy, electric vehicle manufacturing, and battery storage in communities across Michigan.”

Bidirectional Energy and PowerFlex join PG&E's residential V2X program, helping accelerate adoption of new bidirectional technology and giving customers more ways to save money, boost home resilience, and support grid reliability

EVs from Kia, Volvo, Polestar, and Nissan are now approved and eligible for participation

OAKLAND, Calif., Aug. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) today announced a significant expansion of its Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) program, adding several new vehicles and charger options that give customers greater energy resilience and choice in how they power their lives and participate in California's clean energy future.

This includes the addition of Bidirectional Energy and PowerFlex as approved partners, broadening the network of automakers, charger manufacturers, and software solutions providers participating in the program.

Q: What is PG&E announcing?

A: Today, PG&E announced a major expansion of its Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) program, adding new vehicles and charger options through partnerships with Bidirectional Energy and PowerFlex. This expanded network of automakers, chargers, and software solutions gives customers more choices, including the addition of Kia, Volvo, Polestar, and Nissan EVs.

Q: Why is this expansion important for customers?

A: "This expansion is all about choice," said David Almeida, Director, Clean Energy Transportation at PG&E. "By broadening the mix of eligible vehicles and chargers, we're helping our customers access this valuable technology, while also offering them a way turn their EV into a home backup and a grid asset."

The expansion builds on the Ford, Tesla, Chevrolet, GMC, and Cadillac models already on the Eligible Products List.

Q: What is Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X)?

A: V2X technology allows compatible electric vehicles to be used as mobile batteries. With a bidirectional charger, customers can use the electricity stored in their EV battery to:

Provide backup power to their home during outages

Help manage household energy costs

Send power back to the grid during periods of high electricity demand

Support overall grid reliability

PG&E's Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) program offers customers financial incentives to install new bidirectional EV charging technology, which allows a customer's EV to act as a mobile battery, capable of storing electricity that can be used to power their home.

Q: What new options are being added to the program?

A: Customers can now participate through partnerships with Bidirectional Energy and PowerFlex. Newly eligible vehicle and charger combinations include:

Nissan Leaf (2018-2025) with a dcbel Ara charger

Volvo EX90 (2025) with a dcbel Ara charger

Polestar 3 (2025) with a dcbel Ara charger

Kia EV9 (2024 and newer) with a Wallbox Quasar 2 charger

Kia EV6 (2025 and newer) with a Wallbox Quasar 2 charger

These offerings qualify for up to $13,000 in additional incentives being made available through California Energy Commission grant funding, subject to additional eligibility requirements.

Q: Are there any other vehicles being added as part of this expansion of the program?

A: Yes. The expanded program also now includes new EV models from General Motors:

Chevrolet Bolt (2027)

Cadillac Celestiq (2025 and newer)

Cadillac Escalade IQL (2025 and newer)

Customers can also participate through existing options from Ford, General Motors, and Tesla. Capabilities vary by vehicle and charger combination.

Q: Has PG&E deployed V2X technology elsewhere?

A: Yes. PG&E has also advanced V2X solutions for commercial and fleet customers. The company has worked with school districts in Fremont, Oakland, and San Francisco to support the transition to bidirectionally capable electric school bus fleets. These projects help districts reduce emissions and operating costs while providing additional support for California's electrical grid.

Q: What incentives are available for residential customers?

A: Residential incentives include:

$2,500 upfront ($3,000 for customers in disadvantaged communities)

$1,500 Early Adopter Incentive for the first 250 customers to enroll

Q: What about commercial customers?

A: PG&E has supported Fremont, Oakland, and San Francisco school districts in transitioning to bidirectionally capable electric school bus fleets, helping the districts save money and reduce emissions. Today, over 90% of the nation's 500,000 school buses run on carbon-based fuels, releasing over 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases annually, exposing students and communities to harmful fumes. By replacing gas - and diesel-powered vehicles with electric ones, PG&E is helping reduce tailpipe emissions and improving air quality.

title: The newest state on the virtual power plant frontier: Illinois | Planetizen Features
description:
Illinois is the latest example of how a state can embrace virtual power plants and see results almost immediately.
A virtual power plant, or VPP, is a network of resources at homes and businesses that can support the larger community by sending electricity to the grid or by reducing demand.
JB Pritzker signed the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act in January, requiring utilities to develop virtual power plant programs, among other provisions.
Illinois is the fifth state where his company owns virtual power plants, joining California, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Texas.
Mass deployment of virtual power plants has the potential to reduce electricity costs for all Illinois customers, including people not participating, by shifting supply and demand.
text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

Illinois is the latest example of how a state can embrace virtual power plants and see results almost immediately. Last week, Solrite Energy announced its entry into the Illinois market with a program that provides households with battery energy storage for $20 per month and makes the batteries available to support the local power grid.

A virtual power plant, or VPP, is a network of resources at homes and businesses that can support the larger community by sending electricity to the grid or by reducing demand. Solrite, based in Fort Worth, Texas, joins companies such as Base Power and Energywell that market solar and batteries to Illinois customers served by the state’s two largest electricity utilities, ComEd and Ameren.

This comes after Gov. JB Pritzker signed the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act in January, requiring utilities to develop virtual power plant programs, among other provisions. Often, VPPs are batteries connected to solar, but there are many other types, including grid-connected thermostats and water heaters.

I spoke with Regan George, Solrite’s founder and CEO. Illinois is the fifth state where his company owns virtual power plants, joining California, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Texas. George has become adept at describing his business model, which relies on knowledge of the grid, utility regulation and battery technology.

“We put in batteries at residential locations in areas where we have deals with the utilities or the grid operator,” he said. “They can access our batteries [to help] support the grid and then they pay us.”

The company started as Solnova in 2017, specializing in rooftop solar, and then changed its name to Solrite in 2023 as it shifted its focus to virtual power plants. Solrite owns the batteries and solar panels and sets up a system in which customers pay monthly bills for long-term leases for the equipment. It now has about 50 employees and operates systems in about 7,500 homes.

An Illinois customer pays $20 per month under Solrite’s program to have a battery installed, with no installation fee. The customer can also choose to have solar panels installed and pay 12 cents per kilowatt-hour for the electricity generated by the panels, which is a discount compared to the utility’s standard rate.

If the same customer wanted to buy a battery of this size and solar panels, the costs would be substantial, easily exceeding $30,000. Part of the deal is that Solrite gets to use the battery whenever the grid needs a boost, drawing electricity from many batteries to function like a power plant.

Solrite uses a 60-kilowatt-hour battery, which is much larger than a house usually needs, so there is plenty of power to serve that address and send power to the grid. In a power outage, the household can use the battery to keep the lights on, with enough storage to last for days if needed. (For context, households in ComEd territory consume an average of about 20 kilowatt-hours per day.)

The large battery is a distinguishing feature of Solrite’s business model. It’s about four times the size of a Tesla Powerwall unit, which is another battery often used in VPPs. With large batteries in each home, the aggregate size of the power plant could be much larger as the programs gain popularity.

Another distinguishing feature is that Solrite uses batteries designed for use in VPPs, rather than those for which utility networking is a secondary function. The battery manufacturers include Duracell and Sonnen.

“When we’re talking with a retail electric provider or a utility, [it often begins with] them saying, ‘Don’t worry, we won’t use your batteries too much. We’re only going to use them five to 10 times a year,’” George said. “And I have to stop them and say, ‘No, no, no, not our batteries. I want you to use our batteries as much as you possibly can.’” Meanwhile, the homeowner probably won’t notice when electricity is being exported, he said.

Solrite makes its money by selling electricity from its virtual power plant under contracts with utilities and other buyers, and from the monthly fees paid by people leasing solar and batteries. There’s money to be made because VPPs help utilities reduce the amount of electricity they need when demand and prices are highest.

Mass deployment of virtual power plants has the potential to reduce electricity costs for all Illinois customers, including people not participating, by shifting supply and demand. One example is how VPPs can help to reduce the “capacity charge” from grid operator PJM Interconnection. PJM sets this charge as part of its process to ensure its territory has enough power plants to meet peak demand.

The charge is going to be lower, or at least grow less, as gigawatts of VPPs come online, said Will Kenworthy, Midwest regulatory director for Vote Solar, an advocacy group. “If a battery discharges during the handful of summer peak hours that set that charge, the retail electric supplier avoids that cost—and passes the savings on to customers,” he said.

When scaled, VPPs can reduce reliance on centralized power plants, with broad financial and environmental benefits. There is a virtuous cycle here. Illinois passed a law and companies showed up almost immediately. From the companies’ perspective, the state was opening its doors and streamlining the regulatory process for VPPs to operate.

Entering Illinois is “big for us,” George said. “We’re only going to see more and more markets come on.”

Nevada needs additional electric school buses, charging stations and more so the state can grow sustainably, according to clean transportation advocates.

Leaders are calling for more federal funding to support electrification of the transportation sector.

Representative Dina Titus, D-Nevada, said there need to be more bike paths and wider sidewalks to get people out of their cars and improve air quality.

"You need to have more electrification, more public transit. Las Vegas rated 13th-worst metropolitan area by the American Lung Association, and we need to fix that," Titus stressed.

Titus serves on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which recently approved the bipartisan Build America 250 Act by a margin of 62-2. The bill would reauthorize surface transportation funds for the next five years. The proposal still needs full approval in the House before it can head to the Senate.

Olivia Tanager, director of the Toiyabe chapter of the Sierra Club, said improvements to public transportation will help address the affordability crisis and encourage more people to live in the city center near transit, which helps control water-intensive sprawl.

"We need investment in public transportation in order to develop in a way that is transit-oriented to reduce our water footprint and continue the long-term sustainability of life in Southern Nevada," Tanager urged.

Titus called on Congress to keep land use, transportation and air quality in mind when budgeting for the future.

text:
The Healey-Driscoll Administration announced $27.2 million in tax incentives through the Mass Clean Energy Center‘s Climatetech Tax Incentives Program (CTIP). The funding will help 18 Massachusetts-based climatetech companies grow, create jobs, and accelerate the development and deployment of technologies that strengthen the state’s position as a global leader in clean energy solutions that lower costs, reduce pollution, and protect public health.

“Climatetech is creating new opportunities for workers and communities across Massachusetts,” said Governor Maura Healey. “These investments will help companies expand their facilities, hire more workers and grow right here in our state. That means more good jobs, more private investment and more economic growth in communities across Massachusetts.”

“Massachusetts has the talent, ideas and innovation to lead the next generation of climatetech,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “We’re making sure companies have the support they need to take their ideas to the next level and stay here as they grow. That strengthens our economy and creates new opportunities for people and communities across Massachusetts.”

The Climatetech Tax Incentives Program was launched under the Mass Leads Act and builds on MassCEC’s Climatetech Economic Development Strategy and Implementation Plan, a 10-year roadmap to ensure that Massachusetts remains a global climatetech leader. The plan calls for strategic investments in testing and demonstration assets, physical and programmatic support for startups and researchers, and stronger coordination across the ecosystem.

“Massachusetts companies are developing the technologies that will shape the future of energy – from long-duration storage to geothermal and hydrogen,” said Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper. “These incentives will help bring in those technologies to help scale and strengthen the state’s energy system, lower costs, and speed up clean energy solutions.”

“These companies are doing more than growing our economy. They’re tackling some of our toughest climate and energy challenges and showing why Massachusetts is the best place for this type of innovation,” said Economic Development Secretary Eric Paley. “These incentives help companies leading the next generation of climatetech to continue to tap into our talent ecosystem to grow and build here.”

“Massachusetts is producing the solutions to the biggest challenges in climate, energy and affordability. These awardees are all proof of it,” said Ben Downing, Mass Clean Energy Center CEO. “This funding helps them invest in our communities, creating the jobs and technologies that will drive our economy forward while advancing groundbreaking climate solutions.”

The inaugural awards will support 18 companies working across a range of technologies, including energy storage, advanced manufacturing, geothermal energy, clean hydrogen, fusion energy, sustainable aviation fuel, building technologies, and clean transportation. These investments are expected to leverage additional private capital and support the expansion of facilities, research and development, and manufacturing capacity in Massachusetts.

Recipients are located in communities across Massachusetts, from New Bedford and Sunderland to Greater Boston and Devens, underscoring the statewide reach of the state’s growing climatetech sector.

The recipients are:

AeroShield Materials (Waltham, MA): $140,000 – Manufactures aerogel insulation to improve window energy efficiency and reduce HVAC costs.

BT2 Energy (Roxbury, MA): $100,000 – Turnkey developer for EV charging, energy efficiency, and electrification.

Daqus Energy (Woburn, MA): $100,000 – Develops high-energy, low-cost battery cathode materials for next-generation energy storage.

Eden Geopower (Somerville, MA): $100,000 – Uses electric pulse drilling technology to make geothermal energy development faster and more affordable.

Florrent (Sunderland, MA): $120,000 – Produces high-density supercapacitors from biomass waste to support clean energy storage.

Luminous Robotics (Boston, MA): $400,000 – Designs autonomous robotic systems that accelerate solar farm construction and deployment.

Mantel Capture (Cambridge, MA): $100,000 – Develops carbon capture technology for high-temperature industrial boilers, kilns, and furnaces.

Orpheus Ocean (New Bedford, MA): $100,000 – Builds autonomous underwater vehicles that improve seafloor monitoring and data collection.

Pascal Technologies (Cambridge, MA): $100,000 – Develops solid refrigerant cooling systems that reduce cooling costs and improve energy efficiency.

Reframe Systems (Andover, MA): $800,000 – Operates technology-enabled microfactories that produce homes while reducing waste and shortening construction timelines.

REON Technology (Chelmsford, MA): $100,000 – Optimizes the management and performance of battery and solar energy systems to extend their usable life.

Vertical Semiconductor (Somerville, MA): $120,000 – Engineers vertical gallium nitride (GaN) transistors that enable high-efficiency power conversion for AI data centers.

Commonwealth Fusion Systems (Devens, MA): $7,500,000 – Develops high-temperature superconducting magnets that make lower-cost tokamak fusion systems possible.

Electric Hydrogen (Devens, MA): $7,500,000 – Manufactures electrolyzer plants designed to enable low-cost clean hydrogen production at scale.

Electrified Thermal Solutions (Charlestown, MA): $954,000 – Delivers zero-carbon industrial heat using electrically conductive thermal storage “firebricks.”

Form Energy (Somerville, MA): $5,677,258 – Produces grid-scale iron-air batteries capable of providing up to 100 hours of cost-effective energy storage.

Fourth Power (Bedford, MA): $1,546,830 – Creates ultra-high-temperature graphite thermal batteries that convert surplus electricity into long-duration, grid-scale energy storage.

Lydian Labs (Charlestown, MA): $1,784,570 – Converts carbon dioxide and hydrogen into sustainable aviation fuel through a process powered by renewable electricity.

“Energy costs are hitting families hard. That’s why investing in industries of the future isn’t optional, it’s essential,” said State Senator Barry Finegold, Senate Chair of the Joint Committee on Economic Development & Emerging Technologies (D-Andover). “By making a significant commitment to Climatech companies across the Commonwealth, the Mass Leads Act continues to strengthen our state’s push to diversify energy sources and address rising energy costs.”

“These $27.2 million in climatetech tax incentives will help 18 companies bring cutting-edge technologies to the marketplace, all while strengthening our economy and advancing the Commonwealth’s clean energy goals,” said State Representative Carole Fiola, House Chair of the Joint Committee on Economic Development & Emerging Technologies (D-Fall River). “I’m proud to see the investments we made through the 2024 Mass Leads Act deliver meaningful support to companies across Massachusetts, from startups to some of our more promising large-scale clean energy innovators. By continuing to invest strategically in climatetech, we can help keep Massachusetts as a leader in a sector that is critical to our economic competitiveness and our clean energy future.”

text:
The car industry has warned that the planned reform of Germany's renewable energy regulation would restrict bidirectional charging of electric cars and thus threaten their business model, Handelsblatt reported.

Bidirectional charging allows electric vehicles (EVs) to feed stored electricity back into the grid when it is needed by other consumers, effectively helping to balance the grid as battery storage units. The millions of EVs expected to be registered in the coming years are therefore seen as a key flexibility resource for a power system increasingly reliant on intermittent wind and solar generation.

To deal with grid bottlenecks and excess electricity at times of strong solar power output, the government proposes capping the feed-in into to the public grid of new small-scale solar PV installations (smaller than 100 kilowatts) at 50 percent from 2027. The feed-in is currently capped at 60 percent, unless the house has a smart meter. The new rule is meant to incentivise the installation of storage systems, “so that the electricity generated by solar panels at midday - which can no longer be fed into the grid - is stored and then fed back into the grid in the evening,” said the government.

The electricity and car industries now argue that this provision would restrict the entire house connection, regardless of whether a smart meter is in place, and would also affect the feed-in from EV batteries and not only from solar panels.

The rule was originally meant for systems without smart meters, “but now it’s also affecting smart storage systems and electric cars, even when there is spare capacity in the grid and the electricity is actually needed,” Jannik Schall, co-founder of the energy company 1Komma5 Grad, told Handelsblatt.

“This is putting the brakes on a technology that helps drive the growth of electric mobility and the expansion of the grid, and could actually save billions,” said Maximilian Wilshaus, a manager at carmaker VW’s electricity subsidiary Elli. Industry association VDA said it rejects the plans, arguing that the current draft would significantly undermine the economic viability of bidirectional charging technologies, thereby making the technology less attractive to consumers. “Nobody wants that,” a spokesperson told the newspaper.

Germany's cabinet has approved a sweeping overhaul of support for renewable energy projects, ending guaranteed payments for small new rooftop solar systems and cutting compensation for future wind and solar farms hit by grid bottlenecks. The reform has been hailed as a "paradigm shift" by the economy minister, Katherina Reiche, for her stated aim to cut energy transition costs. Environmental NGOs criticised that the reform would create investor uncertainty, jeopardise the expansion of renewable energy sources, slow climate action and weaken Germany’s position as a business location. It will now be debated in parliament, where lawmakers can still make changes.

text:
National EPA powers strengthened

New national environment protection reforms commenced today. They will strengthen the powers of the National Environmental Protection Agency. They will give greater authority to enforce environmental laws and respond quicker to serious breaches.

The reforms include:

higher penalties for the most serious breaches of the law

new environment protection orders which can be issued for up to 14 days in urgent situations to prevent or respond to major breaches. These orders can be extended once for a further 14 days if needed

expanded audit powers to improve monitoring and compliance

Streamlining assessments and increasing certainty

Additional changes commencing today will make project assessment and approval processes more efficient, transparent and consistent under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (EPBC Act). These include:

new provision to allow minor or preparatory works before a final approval decision

updated reconsideration processes

the power for the National EPA CEO to make Rulings

regulations explaining which projects will need to disclose Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions during assessments when the new tests commence

Further information is available on the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water’s website: Environment protection reforms.

First National Environmental Standards

The first four National Environmental Standards were made by the Minister for the Environment and Water on 19 August 2026.

Standards set principles that will need to be met when projects are assessed under the EPBC Act.

The first four Standards are:

Matters of National Environmental Significance

Environmental Offsets

Community Engagement

Data and Information

These standards will not apply to assessments and approval decisions until the new approval tests commence. This will happen on or before 1 December 2026. Further information is available: National Environmental Standards.

The National EPA is developing guidance to help support proponents to navigate the updated assessment processes when they commence.

text:
Energy prices are a concern for Michigan voters ahead of the November election.

For candidates, having a clear position on issues of energy affordability could be vital to their campaigns.

Rising electric bills, eye-popping gasoline prices and pitched local battles over energy-intensive data centers have put energy affordability at the center of the November election in Michigan.

And with a slew of key races on the ballot, candidates who can allay voter concerns about the cost of energy could get a leg up.

The dispute over the Strait of Hormuz — a key pathway through which about a fifth of the world's oil gets out of the Persian Gulf — in the war in Iran has directly led to higher energy prices, a United Nations Conference on Trade and Development report found.

Closer to home, the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) has approved electric rate increases for both of the state's largest investor-owned utilities, DTE Energy and Consumers Energy, in each of the last two years.

Some Michiganders have also taken issue with proposed data centers coming to their communities. The facilities have grown in size and demand with the proliferation of generative artificial intelligence and other cloud functions. Residents have raised concerns about their residential rates increasing as electricity demand increases, although data center proponents note the facilities must pay for their own power under a tariff approved by the MPSC. Still, some critics call for additional protections.

In Michigan’s August primary, some candidates made energy affordability issues a central tenet of their campaigns. In the 7th Congressional District, Will Lawrence won the Democratic primary over two candidates with closer ties to party establishment after making data center opposition a focus. Chris Gilmer-Hill, a Democratic socialist, ousted incumbent state Rep. Helena Scott, D-Detroit, after making the race against the House Democrats' former energy committee chair a de facto referendum on DTE and residential electric rates.

The trend is likely to continue.

"There’s no question about it," said Bernie Porn, a longtime pollster and president of the EPIC-MRA firm in Lansing. The war in Iran, Porn noted, is something Democrats continue to blast on the campaign trail.

A June EPIC-MRA survey, commissioned by pro-clean energy group Climate Power, found 58% of respondents said President Donald Trump's policies have led to higher energy costs.

Candidates forced to reckon with data center antipathy

While Democrats hammer Republicans on high gas prices, GOP candidates have staked out their own energy affordability agenda. Former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate in a race for an open U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, told The Detroit News he supports a one-year moratorium on new data center projects in the state. Such a moratorium would need approval from state lawmakers. The Democratic candidate in the race, former Detroit and Wayne County health administrator Abdul El-Sayed, has called for community protections for water and energy usage for new data center developments, rather than a moratorium. Rogers' campaign didn't return a message seeking comment Aug. 20.

Lawrence's opponent, U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, is also taking aim at data centers, posting a video on social media Aug. 19 where he said decisions on new developments should be made by local communities.

With the at-times heated animosity toward data centers, candidates can't afford to be uninformed on the issue when pressed by constituents and voters, said Sergio Cira-Reyes, climate justice catalyst with the Grand Rapids-based Urban Core Collective.

"I think elected officials have caught on that they need to be ready just in case a data center comes to town," Cira-Reyes said. "They don't want to be blindsided with this huge decision that needs to be made."

Issues of energy affordability, along with more extreme weather events driven by climate change, are hitting closer to home, Cira-Reyes added.

"I would say the politicians who already had sustainability or climate justice as part of their political platform will continue to talk about that," he said. "But there's a growing number of other politicians that are having to brush up."

Race for governor highlights energy stakes

Michigan's next governor will help set the energy policy agenda in Lansing and make two appointments to the MPSC, which sets the rates utility companies can charge customers.

In the gubernatorial race, Democratic Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township outlined different paths to bring down energy costs.

Benson, on her campaign website, proposes "performance-based profit standards so utilities only earn maximum returns when they are delivering reliable, affordable service to Michiganders."

Benson's proposals also include increasing bill credits during power outages, a state program to make home energy efficiency improvements and barring energy cost increases associated with data centers from being passed on to ratepayers.

Benson's campaign did not specify how much she would like to see outage credits increase, but noted that she is eyeing a freeze on utility rates and a possible moratorium on data centers.

On the campaign trail, James has said he would tackle energy costs by repealing the state's Clean Energy & Jobs Act, which targets 2040 as the year when 100% of the state’s energy will come from clean sources. Republicans opposed to that law predict it will increase energy bills, while environmental advocates argue that reversing it would increase household electricity costs.

James has taken particular concern with how the law shifted approval for solar and wind energy projects from local zoning authorities to state regulators. Campaign spokesperson Alyvia Bailey said in a statement, "As Governor (James) will repeal these destructive energy mandates, restore local control and replace the MPSC commissioners who have been rubber-stamping rate increases instead of protecting ratepayers."

Policy experts say the MPSC could take steps to lower costs. Commissioners recently outlined measures to improve energy affordability in a letter sent to outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, although implementing many of the strategies would require legislative approval.

One way to lower energy bills would entail state regulators scrutinizing the return on equity investor-owned utilities earn, said Derrell Slaughter, Michigan Policy Director for Climate & Energy at the Natural Resources Defense Council.

He also called data centers "the elephant in the room," saying the issue "takes the oxygen out of all conversations around everything related to energy and especially around energy affordability." Without greater protections, they have the potential to raise residents' utility costs "exponentially," he said.

description:

According to Bloomberg, power developers are planning 99 new bespoke natural gas plants to power data centers.
Campbell coal-fired power plant (Campbell Plant) in West Olive, Michigan is available to operate.

text:
The “all-of-the-above” approach toward generation development in the U.S. is great for power-hungry data centers, but probably not-so-great for the air we breathe.

Anyone in the clean energy sector could likely have guessed that, but new analysis from BloombergNEF provides some additional data to back it up. According to Bloomberg, power developers are planning 99 new bespoke natural gas plants to power data centers. That’s a huge jump for an industry that only a few years ago was largely focused on replacing capacity from coal plant retirements and providing flexible power to balance renewable generation.

These 99 proposed plants could emit up to 318 million metric tons of carbon dioxide each year, which would mean a 20% increase in U.S. power sector emissions compared to last year’s 1,485 million metric tons overall, per EIA data. This assumes that all 99 of the plants get built, but the potential of such a large increase in emissions underscores how data centers’ appetite for power has revived the gas industry.

Coal is experiencing its own comeback: the DOE issued an emergency order directing the Midwest Independent System Operator (MISO), in coordination with Consumers Energy, to ensure that the 1,420-MW J.H. Campbell coal-fired power plant (Campbell Plant) in West Olive, Michigan is available to operate. The plant was originally scheduled to shut down on May 31, 2025, 15 years before the end of its scheduled design life.

And don’t forget heavy fuel oil (HFO): this week, the Department of Energy (DOE) issued an emergency order permitting PJM Interconnection to continue running the HFO-fired Unit 4 at the Wagner Generating Station in Anne Arundel County, Maryland. PJM had previously requested the order to continue operating the unit beyond its current operating limit to meet high demand in the region.

The grid is getting stretched thin, and emissions goals are getting tossed aside as the reality continues to set in.

Welcome to the Factor This Brief, a weekly collection of energy industry finance and development updates, delivered straight to your inbox on Monday mornings and hosted in a not-so-brief fashion here on Factor This, featuring the people, projects, and technology driving our electric future.

As you may have noticed, I’m filling in for Paul Gerke this week, who is about to return from a well-deserved vacation. Worry not, as Mr. Gerke (and his music taste) will be back in your inbox for the next edition of the Factor This Brief.

As always, thanks for reading. If you catch a piece of news you’d like to see in our weekly roundup, please drop Paul Gerke a line. He’ll be back in action this week with an overflowing inbox as the price to pay for some much-needed time off.

The largest clean energy investment in North American history?

Canada’s Prime Minister, Mark Carney, announced C$10 billion (~$7.26 billion USD) in federal financing to upgrade and expand the hydroelectric Churchill Falls Generating Station; develop the Gull Island hydroelectricity project; unlock co-investment opportunities with the Innu of Labrador in a major new Labrador onshore wind project; and to build transmission lines.

The Canadian government touts these collective projects as the largest clean energy investment in North American history, at nearly C$70 billion ($50.4 billion USD). Together, these projects could deliver 14,000 MW of clean power, which nearly triples the current generating capacity of Churchill Falls.

Bring your own capacity… for data centers?

Households in the PJM and MISO territories are getting an opportunity to get paid for a demand response program supplying power to data centers during periods of high grid stress.

Sunrun, a provider of residential battery storage, solar, and home-to-grid power plants, announced an agreement with Voltus, a distributed energy resource platform, to support Voltus’s “Bring Your Own Capacity” (BYOC) programs for AI hyperscalers.

Under the agreement, Sunrun will provide energy capacity from a portion of its thousands of residential storage-plus-solar systems in PJM and MISO grid regions.

Last year, Voltus announced its BYOC program, which allows large loads like hyperscalers to provide firm, flexible capacity to facilitate data center interconnection and support the grid. As part of that program, Voltus will orchestrate flexible distributed resources — such as batteries and smart thermostats — to reduce energy demand when the grid needs it.

“Meeting growing energy demand requires us to maximize every single electron available across the country,” said Sunrun CEO Mary Powell. “In collaboration with Voltus, we are providing critical capacity from home batteries supported by funding from hyperscalers. This is just the beginning of what distributed energy assets can achieve.”

The Sunrun-Voltus collaboration builds on the recent and separate initiative by Sunrun, Renew Home and Tesla focused on unlocking more than 16.8 gigawatts of flexible capacity from home batteries, solar, smart thermostats, and EVs.

Dimension Energy grows its distributed solar platform

Dimension Energy, a developer, owner, and operator of distributed energy infrastructure, announced that it has secured $857 million of additional capital to accelerate the growth of its distributed solar platform. This follows Dimension’s closing of a $650 million portfolio financing earlier this year.

The $657 million financing will provide construction debt and tax equity financing for a portfolio of 29 distributed solar projects across Illinois, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, totaling 149 MW.

The new capital comprises a $200 million upsize of the company’s corporate credit facility, with lead lenders being Nuveen Energy Infrastructure Credit and funds and accounts managed by HPS Investment Partners, together with a $657 million construction-to-term debt and tax equity financing package.

Dimension currently owns over 600 MW of distributed energy assets operating and under construction. The company argues these financings will support its growth to 1 GW of operating assets by 2028.

LG Energy Solution spins up a new domestic battery plant

Battery manufacturer LG Energy Solution has started production at its brand-new battery plant in Lansing, Michigan. The plant will build battery cells both for energy storage systems and electric vehicles.

The facility produces lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells for energy storage systems (ESS). The cells are integrated by LG Energy Solution Vertech, the company’s U.S. energy storage division, into complete systems for utility, grid-scale storage, and other commercial and industrial applications.

Additionally, the plant will produce nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cells for Toyota’s battery powered vehicles, like the 2027 Toyota Highlander EV.

At full production scale, LG Energy Solution hopes to reach more than 35GWh of annual battery-making capacity. Since 2022, LG Energy Solution has invested more than $2 billion in the Lansing facility, which currently employs about 900 employees. At full capacity, employment is anticipated to grow to 1,700.

title: Poland: Simplification of the Nuclear Investment Process | Insight - Baker McKenzie
description:
New solutions are intended to increase the efficiency of construction of nuclear power plants in Poland and, consequently, to strengthen the country's energy security.
Key assumptions Possibility of phasing nuclear investment: The amendment departs from the previous, rigid solutions, which in practice made it difficult to stage construction works in nuclear investments.
For this purpose, a new solution has been introduced, namely: building permits for the preliminary construction works.
Such permits apply to preliminary construction works covering parts of the nuclear power facility that are not yet capable of functioning independently at a given stage.
Conclusion The discussed amendment is an important step towards improving the process of preparation and implementation of investments in the field of nuclear energy facilities in Poland.
text:
At a glance

On 13 August 2026, the President of Poland signed the amendment to the Act on the Preparation and Implementation of Investments in Nuclear Energy Facilities and Accompanying Investments ("Special Nuclear Act"). The amendment aims to accelerate and simplify the implementation of investments in the area of nuclear energy while maintaining a high level of safety. New solutions are intended to increase the efficiency of construction of nuclear power plants in Poland and, consequently, to strengthen the country's energy security. The amendment is scheduled to take effect 14 days after its publication. Simultaneously, another draft amendment to the same regulation, which also aims to streamline the process of preparation and implementation of nuclear investments (UD382) has already been published and is subject to public consultation and arrangements at the governmental level.

Key assumptions

Possibility of phasing nuclear investment: The amendment departs from the previous, rigid solutions, which in practice made it difficult to stage construction works in nuclear investments. The new law introduces greater flexibility in the investment process, allowing for the division of a project into a series of stages. For this purpose, a new solution has been introduced, namely: building permits for the preliminary construction works. Such permits apply to preliminary construction works covering parts of the nuclear power facility that are not yet capable of functioning independently at a given stage. At the same time, the rules for obtaining an occupancy permit have been adjusted so that they correspond to the phasing approach, including the possibility of obtaining an occupancy permit for a part of the nuclear power facility only. Moreover, it is now clearly determined how the provisions of the Construction Law are to be applied to investments carried out in stages, including those concerning nuclear facilities.

Building permit for preliminary construction works: The amended act defines the types of works that can be considered as 'preliminary construction works' and which may be commenced after obtaining the newly introduced building permit for such works – meaning that the first construction works on the site of a future nuclear facility may commence before obtaining a "regular" building permit for the whole facility. These preliminary construction works have been divided in two groups, however: (i) works that are not significant from the point of view of nuclear safety and radiological protection, and as such not requiring a licence issued by the President of the National Atomic Energy Agency (Państwowa Agencja Atomistyki – PAA) – basic preliminary construction works, and (ii) works that need such a licence for their commencement – qualified preliminary construction works.

Simplified procedure for a building permit regarding preliminary construction works: For obtaining a building permit regarding preliminary works that are not significant from the point of view of nuclear safety and radiological protection, a simplified procedure is envisaged. Now a single administrative procedure will take place before the competent body for architectural and construction administration, i.e., the provincial governor (voivode). This concerns, among others, earth and drainage works, or development of the construction site along with the construction of temporary construction facilities.

Comprehensive procedure for a building permit regarding qualified preliminary construction works: With regard to works that are significant for nuclear safety and radiological protection from the point of view of the nuclear regulatory authority and thus requiring a licence from the President of the PAA, the procedure for obtaining a building permit is more extensive compared to the simplified procedure described above. The issuance of a building permit covering qualified preliminary construction works is conditional upon the investor submitting a licence for the execution of preliminary construction works at the nuclear power facility, issued by the President of the PAA authorising these works in terms of nuclear safety and radiological protection. This solution is aimed at ensuring an appropriate level of supervision and control over the implementation of preliminary works, which is of increased importance from the perspective of investment safety.

Coordination of parallel proceedings: Provisions of the amendment act also ensure proper coordination of parallel proceedings. Conduct of proceedings for the issuance a building permit for a nuclear power facility do not preclude the initiation of proceedings regarding issuance of a building permit covering preliminary construction works for the same facility and vice versa: conduct of proceedings concerning preliminary construction works does not prevent the initiation of proceedings regarding the building permit for the whole nuclear facility. As a result, these changes should translate into a more stable and predictable regulatory environment.

Market context

The current legal regulations contain numerous procedural restrictions, which in practice hinder the efficient preparation and implementation of investments in the field of nuclear energy facilities. These Polish regulations have been largely designed with standard construction investments in mind and do not take into account the specificity of nuclear projects, which are characterized by a high degree of technical complexity, a multi-stage approach and a lengthy implementation process. As a consequence, the existing legal solutions generate additional administrative barriers, which lead to drawing out the procedures, and increase the risk of delays at the investment stage. The introduced amendment is a response to these problems, aimed at better adaptation of the legal framework to the actual course and scale of nuclear investments, and improving the entire process of their preparation and implementation, while maintaining high safety standards. Importantly, new regulations apply to any investment facility, regardless its size; hence also covering potential endeavours regarding Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), since there is no separate legislation covering such installations. Further regulatory improvements are also planned in the form of another amendment to the proceedings before the President of the PAA, in particular regarding the possibility of submitting documentation in English.

Conclusion

The discussed amendment is an important step towards improving the process of preparation and implementation of investments in the field of nuclear energy facilities in Poland. The changes respond to the repeatedly signalled practical problems resulting from a failure to adapt existing regulations to the scale, complexity and long-term nature of such projects. All changes are aimed at reducing regulatory risks and shortening project implementation timeframes, while maintaining high safety standards. The newly adopted changes will not only accelerate the construction of the first Polish nuclear power plant at the Lubiatowo – Kopalino site but will also enable more efficient investment in the second power plant and in relation to SMR projects.
